blocks.text: In the curse of the serpent it is rightly said of the seed of the woman, It shall bruise your head, Gen. III, 15., because in the serpent the head is by far the most important part, and while it is unharmed the serpent rarely succumbs. Isidore, Orig. book 12, ch. 4: Pliny says, if it is to be believed, that the head of a serpent, even if it has escaped with only two fingers' length of body, nevertheless lives. For, as Aelian testifies ^{c)}, τὴν καρδίαν κεκλήρωται ἐπὶ τῇ φάρυγγι [tēn kardian keklērōtai epi tē pharyngi], it has its heart allotted in [III, 241] the throat, near the head, whereas in other animals the heart occupies the middle of the chest. Hence it is that Epaminondas, in order to drive the Thebans straight against the line of the Lacedaemonians, ^{d)} Μέγιστον ἔχιν συλλαβὼν ἔδειξεν αὐτοῖς, καὶ πάντων ἐναντίον τὴν κεφαλὴν τοῦ θηρίου συντρίψας, Ὁρᾶτε, ἔφη, ὅτι τὸ λοιπὸν σῶμα ἄχρηστον, τῆς κεφαλῆς οἰχομένης. οὕτω δὴ ἢν τὰς τῶν πολεμίων κεφαλὰς, τὸ Λακωνικὸν τοῦτο συντρίψωμεν, τὸ λοιπὸν σῶμα τῶν συμμάχων ἄχρηστον. [Megiston echin syllabōn edeixen autois, kai pantōn enantion tēn kephalēn tou thēriou syntripsas, Horate, ephē, hoti to loipon sōma achrēston, tēs kephalēs oichomenēs. houtō dē ēn tas tōn polemiōn kephalas, to Lakōnikon touto syntripsōmen, to loipon sōma tōn symmachōn achrēston.] seized a very large serpent and showed it to them, and having crushed its head in the sight of all, said: You see that, once the head is taken away, the rest of the body is useless. So, if we crush the heads of the enemy, namely this Laconian one, the rest of the body of the allies will be of no use. For this reason the serpent in a fight is almost wholly intent on keeping its head out of danger. Epiphanius in the Physiologus, ch. 15: Ὅλον τὸ σῶμα παραδίδωσι, τὴν κεφαλὴν μόνην φυλάσσει [Holon to sōma paradidōsi, tēn kephalēn monēn phylassei]. And against the Ophites, Heresy 37: Ἐν τῷ διώκεσθαι, γινώσκων ὅτι ἐν τῇ κεφαλῇ αὐτοῦ ἡ πᾶσα ζωὴ αὐτοῦ τυγχάνει, ὅλον τὸ σῶμα ἐνειλήσας ἐπὶ τὴν κεφαλὴν αὐτοῦ κρύπτει μὲν τὸ κρανίον ἑαυτοῦ, παραδίδωσι δὲ τὸ ἄλλο σῶμα· [En tō diōkesthai, ginōskōn hoti en tē kephalē autou hē pasa zōē autou tynchanei, holon to sōma eneilēsas epi tēn kephalēn autou kryptei men to kranion heautou, paradidōsi de to allo sōma] When attacked by someone, since it perceives that its whole life resides in its head, it coils its whole body around its head and hides its skull, but gives up the rest of its body. Chrysostom on Psal. CXIV.: Ὁ ὄφις τὸ λοιπὸν σῶμα προΐεται, ὥστε τὴν κεφαλὴν διασῶσαι [Ho ophis to loipon sōma proietai, hōste tēn kephalēn diasōsai]. The serpent exposes the rest of its body in order to preserve its head. Caesarius, Dialogue 4, Question 192: Ὁ γὰρ ὄφις ὑπὸ βροτοῦ δυνάμει καταλεφθεὶς, ὅλον μὲν τῷ παίοντι τὸ σῶμα περοΐεται, τὴν δὲ κεφαλὴν ἄτρωτον φρουρεῖν μηχανᾶται [Ho gar ophis hypo brotou dynamei katalephtheis, holon men tō paionti to sōma peroietai, tēn de kephalēn atrōton phrourein mēchanatai]. For the serpent, when seized by force by a man, offers its whole body to the one striking it, but tries to keep its head unharmed. Isidore of Pelusium, book 1, Epist. 126: Ὅσαις γὰρ ἂν περιστάσεσι καὶ πληγαῖς ὁ ὄφις συνέχηται, τὴν ἑαυτοῦ φυλάττει κεφαλὴν ἀβλαβῆ· [Hosais gar an peristasesi kai plēgais ho ophis synechētai, tēn heautou phylattei kephalēn ablabē] For whatever mishaps and blows the serpent is beset by, it keeps its head unharmed. And the other Isidore, namely of Seville, Orig. book 12, ch. 4: It offers its whole body in place of its head to those striking it. Tzetzes, Chil. 9, ch. 263:
τυπτόμενος εἰς φόνον, Παντοιοτρόπως τὴν κεφαλὴν τὴν ἑαυτοῦ συγκρύπτει. [typtomenos eis phonon, Pantoiotropōs tēn kephalēn tēn heautou synkryptei.]

Does what the Son of Sirach writes ^{e)} belong here: Οὐκ ἔστι κεφαλὴ ὑπὲρ κεφαλὴν ὄφεως [Ouk esti kephalē hyper kephalēn opheōs]; There is no head above the head of a serpent? I do not think so, because then the sense would be rather obscure. Without doubt, therefore, the author of the book had written in Hebrew לא ראש על ראש הנחש, which should be translated, There is no poison above the poison of the serpent. For ראש means poison as well as head. Thus Deut. XXXII, 33. Their wine, ראש פתנים, the poison of asps. Whoever rendered it the head of asps would be utterly wide of the mark. [III, 242] That poison is partly in the gall, Iob. XX, 14. The gall of asps within him. Pliny, book 11, ch. 37: Let no one be surprised that the gall is the poison of serpents. And book 29, ch. 6: The most careful authors write that this is nothing other than the gall of serpents, and that it reaches them from there through the veins under the spine. Partly also in the teeth, Eccles. XXXIX, 35., and in a certain small bladder under the tongue; therefore Iob. XX, 16. The tongue of the viper shall slay him.
